metadata.title: Claude, Internal Investigation.
metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does Claude gain investigative judgment when it picks up the internal-investigation skill? Take the skill apart, show how it actually runs, judge the design choice — a skill is a framework Claude reads before it starts, not new decision-making power.

beats.narration_text: Read the name 'internal-investigation' and you'd assume Claude picked up judgment about who did what. It didn't. What it picked up was a file — one specification, ordered steps. Let's crack it open and see what's actually inside.

beats.narration_text: Say 'Claude has an internal-investigation skill' out loud and the natural read is that Claude does the investigating — weighs conduct, decides who's at fault. That's the branding. It is not the mechanism.

The model itself doesn't shift when the skill loads or unloads. Delete the folder and Claude loses zero investigative judgment, because there was none to lose — what disappears is one framework to walk through. That's the entire delta.

Here's what a skill actually is, mechanically: one file. Internal-investigation is a folder holding a single SKILL.md — plain-English instructions for running an investigation, step by step, that Claude reads before it does anything.
The execution model is boring on purpose. Claude reads the file top to bottom and walks each step in the written order — no clever branching, no reordering — unless the file itself says branch.

So the skill is a specification, not new judgment — and that's the whole design choice. They optimized for consistency: same steps, same output, every run. What that costs you: anything the file doesn't cover, Claude has no special opinion about.

So internal-investigation never handed Claude judgment about who did what. What it guarantees is smaller, and more useful: every run reads the same file and follows the same ordered steps. That's the trick — replayable process, not fresh opinion.

beats.narration_text: Watch what the flags actually mean, then. Claude marking every irregularity doesn't prove it understood the case — a framework can be executed perfectly and still miss what it was never asked to check. Claude marking nothing doesn't prove nothing happened — it may just be a case the framework doesn't cover. The output tells you about the spec, not about the truth underneath.

So a skill named internal-investigation isn't judgment in a bottle. It's a framework Claude reads before it starts, so the same ordered steps run every time — and everything the framework doesn't cover, that decision is still yours.

props.quote: A skill named internal-investigation isn't judgment in a bottle. It's a framework Claude reads before it starts, so the same ordered steps run every time — and everything outside those steps is still on you.

beats.narration_text: Your turn — a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini today. Pick one process you already run the same way every time — a code review, a shift handoff, a triage. Write yourself a SKILL.md for it: plain language, ordered steps, no branching. Read it back, walk through it before you run it, and name the cases it doesn't cover. Go deeper: which step in that framework should never be handed to an agent, and what breaks the first time it is?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to write a SKILL.md — a single-file, plain-language specification — for a process I already run the same way every time. Walk me through the process in ordered steps, no branching unless I say so, in the exact order Claude would execute them. Then tell me the two or three cases the framework doesn't cover, so I know where I'm still on the hook. My process: [describe your recurring process here — what triggers it, what a good outcome looks like, and what usually goes wrong].
